issues.description: Constructor StockIngredient(String, int, int) is expected by the problem statement and used in examples, but the template only provides StockIngredient(String, int, int, boolean). Problem statement (UML) declares a three-argument constructor; the solution repository implements public StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity); the template repository defines only public StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity, boolean strictValidation). This mismatch prevents instantiating StockIngredient with three arguments (e.g., new StockIngredient("Bacon", 10, 50)) and will cause compilation errors when students or tests use the three-argument form, blocking implementation of SealSaloon.acceptSupplyDelivery and related code.
issues.suggestedFix: Add the expected three-argument constructor public StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity) to the template. Implement it to match the solution behavior (validate/normalize inputs as in the solution) or provide an overload that delegates to the existing four-argument constructor (e.g., public StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity) { this(name, price, quantity, false); }). This will align the template with the problem statement and example usages and prevent compilation errors.

issues.description: Constructor signature inconsistency for the StockIngredient concept: the problem statement (and the solution code) document and use a three-parameter constructor StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity), but the template only provides a four-parameter constructor StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity, boolean strictValidation). Students following the problem text or the example Main will attempt to instantiate StockIngredient with three arguments (e.g., new StockIngredient("Bacon", 10, 50)) and get a compilation error. This mismatch prevents a clear mapping between the required API (problem statement), the example usage, and the template code.
